clue.text: Post Doctor Spooner's medical record

indicators.note: naming the Reverend Spooner tells the solver to swap the opening sounds of the two words the clue yields

blocks.note: a post or station is a base
to doctor accounts is to cook them
the two words just found, said with their opening consonants exchanged

explanation.surface: A doctor sends off a patient's notes in the post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like Spooner's title, but it is also a word to transform: BASE COOK with the initial sounds swapped becomes CASE BOOK.
explanation.definitionFit: A casebook is the volume in which a physician keeps written histories of patients treated.

clue.text: Jaws about first Egyptian pyramid builder

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the following word
about means surrounding, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: chops is slang for the jaws or mouth
the opening letter of Egyptian

explanation.surface: Someone describes the jawline of the first Egyptian king to build a pyramid.
explanation.walkthrough: CHOPS goes around E to give CH-E-OPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheops, also called Khufu, was the pharaoh who had the Great Pyramid of Giza constructed.

clue.text: Garment revealing a little boob - getting forward?

blocks.note: a boob is a blunder, and a small one is a slip
on as in moving on or forward

explanation.surface: A daring outfit that shows a bit of cleavage, and is it rather forward?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boob' and 'revealing' paint a wardrobe malfunction; here boob means a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip-on is any clothing item or shoe pulled on easily without fastenings.

clue.text: Exclamation heard when Brit meets Brit!

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
limey is American slang for a Briton, from sailors given lime juice

explanation.surface: Two Britons bump into each other and one cries out in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: The first Brit shrinks to its abbreviation; the second is the old American nickname. Blimey is a British cry of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Blimey is a colloquial British interjection expressing astonishment, much like gosh.

clue.text: That is blot out and tear in shreds

definitions.text: That is blot out and tear in shreds

indicators.note: out suggests letters thrown out of their places and rearranged
torn into shreds, the letters are broken up and reassembled

blocks.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to wipe something away and rip it to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both builds the answer and describes it: blotting out and tearing up destroy completely.
explanation.definitionFit: To obliterate is to destroy utterly or erase all trace, which blotting out and shredding achieve.

clue.text: Replacing of "ruth" by "quarter"

indicators.note: replacing means putting the letters back in a different place

blocks.note: taken as written, the quote marks ignored

explanation.surface: An editing instruction to swap one word in a text for another.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a substitution instruction, but 'of ruth' is the fodder and 'quarter' the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarter is one of four equal parts of something, which is exactly a fourth.

clue.text: Sort of wear for a single man

blocks.note: single means one
a chessman or draughtsman is a piece

explanation.surface: A style of clothing suitable for a bachelor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single man' suggests a bachelor; here man is a board-game piece.
explanation.definitionFit: One-piece describes swimwear or other garments made as a single item rather than separate parts.

clue.text: Cool megastar

blocks.note: surface reading: a hugely famous celebrity who is effortlessly stylish
setter's reading: a literally enormous star in space with a relatively low surface temperature

explanation.surface: Praise for a hip, enormously famous celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: Cool and megastar both sound like showbiz slang, but they are astronomy: such stars are vast and cooler than the Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: A red giant is a huge late-stage star whose surface is cooler, hence reddish, compared with our Sun.

clue.text: Bloodsucker obtains buck by cunning

blocks.note: a buck is a gymnastic vaulting horse
fly is British slang for sharp or cunning

explanation.surface: A swindler gets money by trickery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buck' looks like a dollar; it is the gym apparatus. 'Fly' as an adjective means wily in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Female horseflies bite livestock and people to feed on their blood, so they are bloodsucking insects.

clue.text: Fit to be tied?

blocks.note: surface reading: so furious one needs restraining
setter's reading: suitable to tie the knot, that is, marriageable

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'fit to be tied' means livid; read literally it means a suitable candidate for marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: An eligible bachelor or spinster is someone considered a suitable and desirable marriage partner.

clue.text: Small boat crank

blocks.note: first meaning: a vessel ferrying people or stores to a larger ship
second meaning: in sailing, a ship liable to heel over

explanation.surface: A dinghy that turns out to be an eccentric.
explanation.walkthrough: Crank looks like an oddball, but in nautical use crank and the answer both describe an unstable vessel that heels easily.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors call an unstable ship that leans readily in the wind either crank or tender.

clue.text: Attribute English try, converted, to front row forward

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: in rugby the props are forwards in the front row of the scrum
E abbreviates English
taken as written

explanation.surface: Rugby commentary: an England try converted, credited to a prop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' and 'converted' are rugby scoring terms, but converted is the anagram signal; the pieces go after PROP.
explanation.definitionFit: A property is a quality or characteristic belonging to something, the same as an attribute.

clue.text: Doubt over dullard, with English limited

indicators.note: in an across clue over means turned back, so the word reads from right to left

blocks.note: an if is a doubt or condition
a nit is a fool
E abbreviates English

explanation.surface: Uncertainty about a dimwit whose English is poor.
explanation.walkthrough: FI (IF turned back) + NIT + E.
explanation.definitionFit: Finite means having bounds or an end, so it is limited rather than infinite.

clue.text: Neat Gemini anagram for "repeat"

indicators.note: the setter names the device outright: rearrange the preceding letters

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; Gemini is also this puzzle's setter

explanation.surface: The setter Gemini boasts of a tidy anagram of their own name.
explanation.walkthrough: An unusually candid clue: the setter's pseudonym is part of the fodder and the word 'anagram' is the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingeminate is a rare literary verb meaning to say again or reiterate, from Latin geminus, twin.

clue.text: National waterway? Yes, indeed!

blocks.note: surface reading: some country's chief canal, followed by an emphatic affirmative
setter's reading: the enthusiastic reply calls the waterway splendid, and that grand one is named as such in Ireland, China and Venice

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a canal belongs to the nation and is answered with gusto.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation answers the question by praising it as grand; Ireland's main canal and China's great imperial one both bear the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grand Canal is the name of the national canal of Ireland and the vast ancient waterway of China.

clue.text: Narrow agreement

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to make or become smaller
second meaning: a noun, a binding legal deal

explanation.walkthrough: Narrow looks like an adjective modifying agreement, but it is the verb, stressed on the second syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscles contract when they shrink in size, while a contract is a formal binding deal between parties.

clue.text: Locksmith?

blocks.note: surface reading: a tradesman who makes and repairs door locks
setter's reading: a craftsman who works on locks of hair

explanation.walkthrough: Locks here are tresses of hair, and a smith is a skilled worker.
explanation.definitionFit: A coiffeur is a hairdresser, a French term for one who styles and cuts hair.

clue.text: Is taking issue without showing contempt

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: to issue from something is to derive from it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone takes issue with a point but doesn't show disdain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking; here it is the old sense of outside, as in the hymn's 'a green hill far away, without a city wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Derisive means mocking or scornful, so a derisive laugh is one showing contempt.

clue.text: Being alert, could be soon seen to

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters may become something else once rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Being watchful means a problem may be dealt with quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on one's toes is an idiom for staying ready, watchful and quick to react.

clue.text: Girl's collar

blocks.note: first meaning: a woman's name
second meaning: a wide, round lace collar on a low neckline

explanation.surface: A collar belonging to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's looks possessive; it stands for 'is', joining two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertha is a girl's name, and a bertha is a broad falling collar on Victorian dresses.

clue.text: Local litter, scattered about, hasn't been what?

definitions.text: Local litter, scattered about, hasn't been what?

blocks.clueFragment: Local litter, scattered about, hasn't been what?
blocks.note: surface reading: a grumble about rubbish strewn round the neighbourhood
setter's reading: the question asks what has failed to happen to the rubbish, namely its disposal in a rubbish receptacle

explanation.surface: Someone complains about rubbish strewn round the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer fills the blank: litter lying about has plainly not been put in the bin, the British word for a rubbish container.
explanation.definitionFit: Binned means thrown away into a rubbish receptacle, which is what scattered litter has failed to be.

clue.text: Overtime imposed on staff - walked over again!

blocks.note: split as over, giving RE (about, as in a row over money), and time, abbreviated T
a staff is a rod or stick

explanation.surface: Workers forced to do extra hours, and they trudged back over the same ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overtime' must be split into two words. In a down clue 'imposed on' puts the first pieces above ROD.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrod is the past tense of retread, to tread or walk along the same path once more.

clue.text: Food spat out? Quite the opposite!

blocks.note: a spat is a petty quarrel, a tiff
the clue's closing words tell you to take the opposite of out

explanation.surface: A meal spat out in disgust, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spat' looks like a verb, but it is a noun. Tiffin is a light meal, a word from British India.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiffin is a light midday meal or snack, a term from British India still used in South Asia.

clue.text: Not the main concern of party policy

blocks.note: a side is a party in a dispute
a party line is its policy

explanation.surface: A political party's policy is not its chief worry.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideline is a secondary activity or business pursued alongside one's principal occupation.

clue.text: Boy of few years turning to drink

indicators.note: turning means the word is read backwards

blocks.note: ale is beer
six years is a young age, a few years

explanation.surface: A young lad is taking to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Few years' stands for a small child's age; the reversed number then follows the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexis is a given name, traditionally borne by males, from Greek meaning helper or defender.

clue.text: Fellow takes nearest roundabout to Pinner

indicators.note: a roundabout is a circular route, so the letters are spun into a new order

blocks.note: F abbreviates fellow
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man takes the closest traffic roundabout to get to Pinner, a suburb of north-west London.
explanation.walkthrough: Pinner looks like the London place name; it is a thing that pins, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A fastener holds things together, as a pin does, so it is a whimsical pinner.

clue.text: Fixed course back to island republic

indicators.note: back means the word is read from the end to the start

blocks.note: a rut is a fixed routine or groove
a key or cay is a low island, as in the Florida Keys

explanation.surface: A set route leading back to an island nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Island republic' wants to be one phrase, but the island is a separate piece and only 'republic' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Turkey is a republic, founded by Atatürk in 1923, spanning Anatolia and a corner of Europe.

clue.text: Arrested? That's not very clever!

blocks.note: first meaning: held back or slowed in development
second meaning: a dated, now offensive term for intellectually slow

explanation.surface: Getting yourself arrested was a foolish move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrested' suggests the police; it means checked or delayed, as in arrested development.
explanation.definitionFit: To retard is to delay or hold back, and the dated adjective was used for someone slow-witted.
